en: The *Sūtra of the Girl Rucirā*, translated by an unknown person, now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin:
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
He was preaching the sutras for the fourfold assembly of disciples.

At that time, in the kingdom, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada took a wife for his son; he obtained the daughter of an elder named Yujia (Yaśodharā), who was exceptionally beautiful and outstanding. However, she did not observe the rites of a wife and treated her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband with contempt.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his wife deliberated, saying:
"This wife is disobedient; how should she be instructed?
If we were to apply corporal punishment, it would not be in accordance with the Dharma."
"If we do not instruct and admonish him, his transgressions will increase day by day.
The elder deliberated, saying,
"Only the Buddha can transform him."
At dawn the next morning, he dressed in formal attire and went to where the Buddha was. Bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed him, saying:

“I have taken a wife for my son and obtained the daughter of an elder; however, she is exceedingly arrogant and does not observe the decorum due to a wife. I pray only that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and our disciples, and tomorrow, at our invitation, come to our home to preach the sutras so that their minds may be opened and enlightened.”
The Buddha accepted the invitation, and the elder, filled with joy, paid homage to the Buddha and returned home.

Upon reaching his residence, the elder prepared an extensive array of provisions and magnificently adorned the seats. At dawn, when the Buddha arrived at the elder’s house, the elder greeted him with great delight and invited the Tathāgata to enter. Once the assembly was seated, everyone paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side. After the Buddha had finished his meal, he preached the sutra for them; yet, Yuyé alone remained arrogant and did not come forth.

The Buddha, mindful of her and moved by compassion, manifested great supernatural power, transforming the householder’s home entirely into the color of crystal; inside and out they reflected one another without any obstruction.

When Yaya beheld the Buddha’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the hair on her body stood on end and she trembled with fear. She immediately came forth to prostrate before the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side; with palms joined and head bowed, she remained silent, unable to speak.
The Buddha said to Yuye:
"A woman is not upright because her facial features are handsome; she is not upright for failing to obey her husband. To have an upright mind and upright conduct—that is true uprightness."
Within the body of a woman there are ten evils that she does not perceive herself. What are these ten evils?

First, being conceived in the womb makes her difficult for her parents to nourish; second, while pregnant she is filled with anxiety and sorrow; third, at birth her parents are not joyful; fourth, raising her brings no pleasure; fifth, her parents must follow her constantly without regard for the proper occasion; sixth, she is fearful of others everywhere; seventh, she is perpetually anxious about marriage; eighth, once born, she is separated from her parents; ninth, she is always afraid of her husband; tenth, she lacks self-mastery—these are called the ten evils.
Yujie, filled with fear and trepidation, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha will teach me the etiquette of women; what are its particulars?”
The Buddha said to Yuye:
"When a wife serves her husband, her parents-in-law, and her elders, there are five virtues and three evils.
What are the five virtues?"

First, she lies down last and rises early, offering the finest food first; second, she does not harbor resentment when struck or scolded; third, she directs her whole heart toward her husband and does not commit sexual misconduct; fourth, she prays for her husband’s long life and serves him with her person; fifth, when her husband travels afar, she manages the household without a divided mind—these are the five virtues.
What are the three evils?

First, she treats her husband with contempt and does not obey her elders; she eats fine food herself, goes to bed early before dusk, and does not rise when the sun comes up; when her husband instructs or rebukes her, she responds with glaring eyes and anger.
Second, seeing that her husband is displeased, her mind is constantly ruined, and she longs for other men.
Third, she wishes for her husband to die early so that she may remarry; these are the three evils.
Yujia remained silent, having no words with which to answer.
The Buddha said to Yujia:
"In this world there are seven kinds of wives; I shall describe them for you, so listen attentively and with a focused mind."

First, the mother’s wife; second, the sister’s wife; third, the wife of a spiritual friend; fourth, the wife of a wife; fifth, the wife of a slave; sixth, the wife of an enemy; and seventh, the wife who has taken one’s life.
"Do you understand now? Yujia replied,
"I do not grasp this meaning."
The Buddha said:
"Listen well; I shall now explain it to you.
What is meant by 'mother and wife'?"

She loves her husband as a mother loves her child, nurturing him day and night at the proper times; her heart is always filled with compassion and she never grows weary, cherishing her husband as if he were her own son—this is what it means to be a "motherly wife."
What is a sister-wife?

She serves her husband with the utmost reverence and sincerity; she regards him as a brother or a younger sibling, sharing his vital breath and physical form, being a kinsman of bone and blood with whom there is no duplicity of heart. She honors and values him as a sister serves her elder brother—this is called a sister-wife.

What is a wife who is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)? She serves her husband with reverence and sincere obedience; she is devoted and affectionate, never wishing to be apart from him. She constantly informs him of private matters and acts without transgression. She instructs him in virtuous deeds to increase his wisdom and insight. She is intimate and loving, desiring to lead him across the world [to liberation]. Like a true spiritual friend, such is the wife who is a spiritual friend.
What is meant by a "woman of women"?

She honors great beings, exhausting her feelings and fulfilling her conduct without reserve; she purely cultivates the rites of a wife, never neglecting them; she advances without violating righteousness and retreats without losing propriety; she prizes constant harmony—this is called a woman of women.

What is meant by a "slave-wife"? One whose mind is always fearful and cautious, not daring to be arrogant; who is loyal and filial, exhausting herself in her duties; whose speech is not coarse and whose body is not negligent; who restrains herself with propriety as a subject serves a king; whom her husband honors and favors, yet she does not become haughty; who, if she receives a beating, respectfully accepts it, and if she sees him revile or insult her, remains silent without retort; who endures the hardships and pleasures of her body with a single-minded devotion, cultivating the path of a wife without regard for food or clothing; and who serves her husband as if serving her master—this is called a slave-wife.

What is a wife who is like an enemy? She sees her husband with no joy and constantly harbors anger; day and night she prays and wishes for him to be far away from her. Though they are husband and wife, her heart is always as if on loan. Her hair is disheveled and she sleeps restlessly, showing no fear or avoidance. She does not engage in productive labor to raise her children; she conducts herself with lewdness and knows no shame. She falls into sinful ways and brings disgrace upon her kin. Husband and wife loathe one another, and she utters curses wishing for his death—this is called a wife who is like an enemy.

What is a wife who takes one’s life? She does not sleep day or night, harboring a poisonous heart as she watches for her opportunity. She devises various means to distance herself from him, wishing to give him poison but fearing he might discover her. Her heart is outwardly loyal while her affections are elsewhere; she hires someone to harm him, or dispatches a paramour to lie in wait and assassinate him. Once the husband is dead, she remarries—this is exactly what she desires. This is called a wife who takes one’s life.
The Buddha said to Yuye: "A woman who possesses such virtue shall attain a distinguished reputation;

her extended family and nine branches of kin shall all share in her glory. Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits shall protect her person, ensuring she does not suffer unjust calamities, and her wealth and treasures shall increase daily. After her life ends, her every wish shall be fulfilled as she is reborn in the heavens, where palaces and bathing pools appear spontaneously and where devas rejoice. When her lifespan in heaven is exhausted, she shall return to the human world, always born into the lineage of wealthy and noble princes, beautiful and graceful, honored and revered by all."
That wicked wife shall incur an evil reputation;

in her present life she shall find no peace, as ghosts and spirits frequently haunt her household to cause illness and misfortune, seeking even to reach the divine deities. She shall inevitably meet death and attain no longevity;
plagued by nightmares and terrors, her aspirations shall not be fulfilled, and she shall encounter many calamities, including those of water and fire.
Day after day they are terrified; after ten thousand such lifetimes, their spirits receive new forms. Upon death, they enter the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the realm of animals.
Their bodies are stunted and short, with throats as narrow as needles. They lie upon iron beds for many thousands of millions of kalpas.
Once their retribution is exhausted, they are reborn into evil households—poor, naked, and destitute, lacking even silk or hemp, struggling in constant urgency.
We urgently urge one another to exert ourselves, for from birth until death there is no glory or splendor;
performing good brings good, while committing evil brings its own retribution—such is the nature of good and evil, and it is not false.
The Buddha said to Yuye, "These are the seven types of wives; which conduct do you employ?
Yuye shed tears and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"I was originally foolish and did not obey my husband's honor. From this day forward, I shall act as a servant wife; for the remainder of my life, I dare not be arrogant.
She then knelt before him and requested to receive the ten precepts and the three refuges—taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus.

First, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual misconduct; fourth, not speaking falsely; fifth, not drinking intoxicants; sixth, not using harsh speech; seventh, not engaging in frivolous speech; eighth, not being jealous; ninth, not harboring anger; tenth, believing that good yields good—these are called the ten precepts, which are the practice of the upāsikā.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, the disciples all wished to return. The Elder Anāthapiṇḍada and his retinue rejoiced, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew.
Yajñadevī knelt upright and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I was originally foolish and my husband was arrogant; now, having received the World-Honored One’s transformation and guidance, our minds have been opened and enlightened."
The Buddha said to Yuye:
"From this day forward, I shall protect and uphold your family. Yuye replied:
"So be it! We shall receive the Buddha's instructions and dare not disobey.
Having bowed their heads at his feet in salutation, they accepted them and withdrew to return home.
The Sūtra of the Jade Maiden (Yenuye jing)
